title: The Agent Harness: What It Is and Two Ways to Build One
gist: Production AI agents are 'model + harness', and the harness (memory, tools/MCP, routing, cost caps, observability) is where most engineering effort goes; the operations half is essentially DevOps. The article builds the same finance agent (FinBot) on AWS Bedrock AgentCore Harness (Harness-as-a-Service) and on self-managed LangChain + Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) on Kubernetes, arguing both deliver the same capabilities and the choice is about who operates it, cost structure, governance and portability.

insights.claim: The gap between a demo AI agent and a production agent is the surrounding harness (memory, tool access, model routing, guardrails, cost controls, tracing), which consumes most engineering time and almost none of which comes from the model itself.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Value and spend in agentic AI accrue to infrastructure/tooling layers around models, not just to model providers.
insights.quote: Almost none of that capability comes from the model. It comes from everything you build around the model
insights.locator: A production agent has to stay up

insights.claim: An agent should be framed as a model plus a harness (a framing attributed to Vivek Trivedy): the model is the engine providing power, while the harness is the chassis, brakes and dashboard that make it a shippable product.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Useful mental model for sizing the non-model agent-infrastructure market alongside foundation-model spend.
insights.quote: if you’re not the model, you’re the harness
insights.locator: Agent = Model + Harness

insights.claim: The term 'agent harness' only caught on in 2026, but the underlying work (gluing tools, tuning prompts, adding retries and logging) is not new; naming it lets teams design it deliberately instead of accumulating one-off fixes.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Emerging category naming ('harness', 'HaaS') signals a new product category vendors will market into.
insights.locator: Agent = Model + Harness

insights.claim: The model still matters: a stronger model lifts everything above it, but an AI agent is a product, and building it takes far more than wrapping a model in an API.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Model quality and harness tooling are complements; neither layer captures all value.
insights.quote: An AI agent isn’t a model, it’s a product.
insights.locator: I want to be careful here

insights.claim: Teams should grow the agent harness incrementally with the agent rather than gold-plating it up front, since value comes from the job getting done.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Suggests adoption of harness tooling will be gradual and usage-driven rather than big upfront platform purchases.
insights.locator: Key Takeaways

themes.theme: Harness splits into dev and ops

insights.claim: Agent harness capabilities split into a development half (memory across sessions, tools and MCP, retrieval, prompts, orchestration) and an operations half (observability, evaluation, guardrails, routing, drift and cost monitoring, deployment, scaling).
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Map vendors against each half to see where the agent-infra stack is consolidating.
insights.locator: The Two Halves of a Harness

insights.claim: The operations half of an agent harness is essentially DevOps repurposed for AI agents, so existing DevOps/observability skills and tools transfer directly.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Incumbent DevOps, observability and gateway vendors are positioned to extend into agent operations.
insights.quote: The operations half is essentially DevOps, wearing a new hat.
insights.locator: I want to be careful here

insights.claim: Unified model access, cost control and observability are the three operational capabilities that, in the author's experience, decide production-readiness of an agent faster than anything else.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Gateway, FinOps and LLM-observability tools are the first harness components enterprises will buy.
insights.locator: The Demo: Building FinBot

insights.claim: Harness-as-a-Service offerings (AWS AgentCore, Google Vertex AI Agent Engine, Azure AI Foundry Agent Service, LangGraph Platform) and self-managed stacks (LangChain or LlamaIndex plus Agent Router or LiteLLM on Kubernetes) deliver the same building blocks; the difference is who assembles, operates and gets paged for them.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers compete on managed agent runtimes while open-source stacks compete on portability; capabilities are converging, so differentiation shifts to operations and lock-in.
insights.quote: What changes isn’t the parts. It’s who assembles them and who gets paged when they break.
insights.locator: What differs is how those blocks

insights.claim: HaaS is simpler to budget with a predictable vendor bill, while a self-managed agent harness can come out cheaper at scale once operating costs are paid either way.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Expect large-scale agent deployments to migrate toward self-managed stacks, pressuring managed-runtime margins at the high end.
insights.quote: HaaS is simpler to budget; self-managed can come out cheaper at scale, once you’re paying to operate it either way.
insights.locator: Choosing Where to Sit on the Spectrum

insights.claim: Governance requirements push some enterprises to keep agent guardrails, audit trails and data paths inside their own boundary, with some required to run everything in their own VPC.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Regulated-industry demand supports self-hosted and open-source agent infrastructure.
insights.quote: Some enterprises must run all of this in their own VPC.
insights.locator: Choosing Where to Sit on the Spectrum

insights.claim: A self-managed gateway stack is cloud-agnostic: moving from EKS in front of Bedrock to GKE in front of Vertex leaves agent code and its endpoint unchanged, with only backend schema, model IDs, credentials, workload identity and deployment config reconfigured.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Open gateways reduce switching costs between cloud model providers, weakening hyperscaler lock-in.
insights.locator: The examples run on EKS

insights.claim: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides Runtime, Memory, Identity, Gateway, Observability, Code Interpreter and Browser primitives, and AgentCore Harness wires them via two calls (CreateHarness, InvokeHarness) with a Firecracker microVM per session.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: AWS is packaging agent infrastructure as a config-driven managed service to capture agent workloads.
insights.locator: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gives you

insights.claim: AgentCore Harness can export a config-defined agent to editable Strands code running on the same runtime, reducing the lock-in penalty of starting on config.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Lowers the barrier for teams to start on AWS's managed harness and stay on its runtime as needs grow.
insights.quote: Config for the boring eighty percent, code for the twenty percent that’s actually specific to you.
insights.locator: When config runs out of road

insights.claim: AgentCore supports Bedrock, OpenAI, Gemini and any LiteLLM-compatible provider, can switch provider mid-session without losing context, and stores third-party keys in AgentCore Identity's token vault.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Even the hyperscaler's managed harness is multi-model, commoditizing model choice at the routing layer.
insights.locator: On AgentCore

insights.claim: AgentCore enforces per-invocation hard caps on agent loops (maxIterations defaulting to 75, maxTokens, timeoutSeconds) and automatically ships traces, logs and metrics to CloudWatch after a one-time account setup.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Built-in cost caps and tracing are key selling points of managed harnesses versus DIY instrumentation.
insights.locator: Cost Control

insights.claim: Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway), built on Envoy Proxy and CNCF Envoy Gateway, exposes one OpenAI-compatible endpoint across many providers with token-based rate limiting, routing and failover, and holds provider credentials at the gateway so agents never see keys.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: The OpenAI-compatible API has become the de facto interface for AI gateways, a standard layer between agents and model vendors.
insights.locator: Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) is

insights.claim: Managed per-invocation caps stop a runaway loop but only a gateway-level token budget can enforce per-tenant limits, e.g., rejecting requests with HTTP 429 once a user's daily token budget is spent.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant SaaS builders need gateway-level FinOps controls that managed agent runtimes do not natively provide.
insights.quote: Only the second one knows what a tenant is.
insights.locator: AgentCore caps the agent

insights.claim: Self-managed agent observability converges on OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* semantic conventions, letting gateway spans and app spans (via tools like OpenLIT, Langfuse, Phoenix) flow to one collector and keeping metrics portable across providers.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Standardized GenAI telemetry commoditizes instrumentation and shifts competition among LLM-observability vendors to backends and analysis.
insights.locator: Both emit the same gen_ai.* vocabulary

insights.claim: OpenTelemetry GenAI instrumentation captures no message content by default, and OpenTelemetry's own LangChain instrumentation was still beta at time of writing, so self-managed tracing requires extra configuration and raises prompt-data access concerns.
insights.speaker: Trista Pan
insights.so_what: Maturity gaps in open agent observability are a near-term advantage for managed harnesses that trace the loop automatically.
insights.quote: message content is off by default
insights.locator: The OpenTelemetry project ships its own
